This feature fires on the key noun that names or headlines the main subject of a technical or scientific passage—i.e. the title-like token that introduces a new concept or section.

explanations.explanation: This neuron is a “headline/title‐style” detector—it lights up on tokens that commonly occur as the first or key words in section headings and article titles (e.g. Put, Which, United, Pew, suffixes in names, etc.), signaling that the model is processing a title or headline segment.

This neuron seems to be a kind of “content‐word salience” detector.  It lights up whenever the model encounters a lexically rich token—whether a key noun (massage, Industries, Adapters, Carmalita), an adjective/adverb carrying descriptive weight (delicate, vivid, danger, chaotically), or even the structural markers that label headings, lists or citations (periods in “Pet. Docket,” docket numbers like 446/559, chapter-list punctuation).  In short, it flags the tokens that bear the core topic or boundary information in a wide variety of contexts.

This feature fires on “weird” contiguous character chunks—low-frequency n-grams or pure‐whitespace runs that don’t look like ordinary words.  You see it light up on odd bigrams/trigrams inside names (e.g. “dn” in a handle, “HU” in McHUGH, “Szech” in Szechuan, “reng” in Derengoski, “ff” in Steffy), on repeats in DNA (“AA”), and even on pure-space tokens (indents).  In other words, it picks out rare or non-dictionary substrings (including multi-space runs) within otherwise normal text.

This feature lights up on the trappings of a news-reporting style—formal event-describing verbs (endured, remained, poised, revealed), evaluative adjectives (horrific), hedging adverbs (reportedly) and sentence-ending punctuation—i.e. the register of factual, often sensational, reportage.

explanations.explanation: This feature fires on the initial subtoken of “prominent” words—proper names, titles, headings or other label‐like tokens—i.e. it marks the start of a named entity or headline/section word (often signaled by capitalization, punctuation or being the first piece of a hyphenated compound).

This feature fires on words used as section‐ or document‐level headings or titles—i.e. tokens that kick off new posts, articles, Q&As, recipes, legal opinions, etc., marking the start of a distinct content block.

This feature is a sub‐token n-gram detector: it lights up on distinctive multi-letter sequences (e.g. “ough,” “lank,” “rit,” “apt,” Cyrillic “ил/еб/ор,” etc.) that often occur in proper names or specialized vocabulary across languages.

This feature detects section‐header labels—phrases or keywords followed by a colon—that signal the start of a new labeled block (e.g. “Tags:”, “Product Info:”, “Tutorial Details:”) across varied document types.

This neuron lights up on tokens that serve as structural or section‐boundary markers in formal text—whether it’s the horizontal‐rule “---” that kicks off an abstract or section, the opening “Let” of a math statement (or similar discourse‐startup words like “so” at a sentence’s start), or even citation‐volume numbers like “121”—in short, it detects the beginnings of new segments or formal statements in academic/mathematical writing.

This neuron fires on the “heading” or “label” words that kick off title-like lines—i.e. the product/model specifiers, tech acronyms and category nouns or adjectives you see at the start of listings, tutorials or announcements (GT, USB, workshops, phones, systems, Rainbow, VR, DAC, wooden, constructed, etc.). It marks the token that names the topic or feature of that segment.

explanations.explanation:
1. The single‐letter function symbol “f” in formal algebraic/math expressions.  
2. The heading token “Terms” in “Terms & Conditions” sections of legal agreements.  
3. Court‐reporter volume numbers in case citations (e.g. “234 F.2d 62…”).  
4. Single‐letter variable names (like “s”) in algebraic equation contexts.  
5. Numeric entries in a structured tabular/CSV‐style dataset (rows of measurements).  
6. The word “decorator” as it appears in Python package distribution metadata (dist-info).  
7. Skill name prefixes in video-game descriptions (e.g. “Crushing Blow”).  
8. Java class names in code, specifically “SimpleClass.”  
9. The SIMD Boolean vector variable “b16” in JavaScript (SIMD.js) code.  
10. Zero values in SVG path data strings (the “d” attribute).  
11. The literal software name “LAMMPS” in molecular‐dynamics input scripts.  
12. The abbreviation for a legal reporter series “L.R.R.M.” in case citations.  
13. Elixir module names beginning with “L” (e.g. “LoomWWRegister”).  
14. The word “Filed” marking filing information in court‐case headers.  
15. Another court‐reporter volume number in citations (e.g. “524 F.2d…”).  
16. Brand or product name prefixes (“Gr” in “Gracie Grooves Dance Studio Leggings”).  
17. The party‐separator “v.” in legal case titles (e.g. “Smith v. Jones”).

This feature fires on tokens that signal structural or navigational elements in web‐style text—i.e. the first word of section headings, bylines or timestamps, link or “jump” prompts, and bullet‐list labels. It essentially marks those tokens that frame an article’s layout and metadata (dates, “Related,” “Explore,” “Promotes,” etc.).

This neuron flags the little “label” tokens that kick off structured metadata or references in formal/technical texts—e.g. the initial word or number in a legal citation (“Cite”), a parenthesized area code (“(318)”), a module name in an electronics file, author initials or case numbers, journal‐name tokens, “NOT FOR PUBLICATION” markers, etc. In short, it detects the leading token of document identifiers or reference headers.
This feature fires on the legal term “express” as used in the boilerplate warranty disclaimer (“any express or implied warranties”) that appears in open-source license headers.

This feature is a subword‐stem detector: it fires on the second piece of split tokens that carry the core meaning of a word (e.g. “rowth” in “growth,” “intestinal” in “gastrointestinal,” “itoring” in “monitoring,” “courses,” “magnetic,” “gastric,” “maintenance,” “progression,” “marijuana,” “laptop,” etc.). In effect, it recognizes the morpheme or root segment that encodes the main semantic content across both scientific/technical and everyday language.

explanations.explanation: This neuron is a subword‐level trigram detector: it fires on mid-word character sequences (e.g. “aph,” “orn,” “anz,” “ess,” “ert,” “éd,” “ăn,” “äl,” “ил,” etc.) found across multisyllabic content words in various languages (think “semaphore,” “pornography,” “Tanzanite,” “fédéral,” “până,” “jälkeen,” “весьма,” “kertoneet,” “вилучення,” etc.).

This feature fires on tokens that serve as document‐structure markers—words (often capitalized “In,” titles like “Abstract,” headings, job‐titles or legal headers) that signal the start of a new section, title, or metadata block.

This neuron consistently lights up on the initial BPE piece of longer content words—e.g. “annat,” “order,” “bere,” “ace,” “camp,” “lum,” “wy”—across languages. In other words, it flags the subword stem at the start of a multi-piece word.

This feature fires on the “big” technical nouns and identifiers you see in code or specs—especially short, uppercase or Camel-case tokens (single‐letter or acronymic names, class/struct/macros, technical keywords like “magnetic,” “Validation,” “Audio,” “MD5,” etc.). It marks the key domain‐specific terms that name types, macros or core concepts in programming and technical documents.

This feature consistently lights up on the single, most salient “head” token in a heading or title—whether it’s the company type in a case name (“Insurance”), the ranking in a business list (“500”), a named event (“Friday”), a metadata label (“Version”), a date numeral (“31”), a color‐code marker (“#”), or a patent’s key noun (“combustion”). In other words, it picks out the document’s core subject identifier in headers across legal, business, technical and HTML contexts.

This feature is basically a suffix detector: it lights up on tokens that form the final few letters of a word (especially common morphological endings like ­ancy, ­ion, ­ive, ­ity, ­ual, etc., and the analogous endings in names and titles).

This feature is a “subword‐split” detector: it fires on the individual WordPiece/BPE fragments (either the first or second piece) whenever a capitalized proper name or multi-syllable noun is split into exactly two tokens (e.g. “Super”∕“bike,” “Charl”∕“eston,” “Cul”∕“inary,” “Americ”∕“a,” “Tenn”∕“essee,” etc.).

This feature flags content-bearing, morphologically complex words—especially technical terms formed with derivational suffixes (–ion, –ed, –ly, etc.) or hyphenated compounds—common in scientific/technical prose.

This neuron is a subword‐morpheme detector: it lights up whenever it sees common Latin/Greek root or affix fragments (e.g. “quer” in conquer/Conqueror, “und” in conundrum, “cent” in concentration, “ic” in colic, “ith” in lithographic, “uan” in Lithuanian, “an” in argumenta, etc.), regardless of the surrounding domain or language.

This neuron fires on the very first, highly-salient word of a title or headline (e.g. the opening capitalized token in blog-post titles, list headings or article headings). It flags the word that kicks off a section or headline.

This feature fires on boilerplate legal-and-licensing language—short, standardized disclaimers and metadata (e.g. court-opinion citation rules like “unpublished,” corporate copyright notices with “affiliates,” and distribution clauses such as “distributed” in software license headers).

This neuron flags subword tokens that are the initial fragments of capitalized terms—whether proper nouns (places, people), acronyms, or domain-specific word roots (as in titles and technical headings).

This neuron fires on the “lead‐in” words of multiword names and titles—especially capitalized spatial/prepositional or relational tokens (Under, In, Of, Near, Far) and key title nouns (Walk, Progress)—marking the start of compound proper nouns or named‐entity phrases.
This feature fires on the opening single‐quote that immediately follows the “abstract:” label in these scientific papers, marking the start of the quoted abstract text.

This neuron is basically a character‐sequence detector: it spikes whenever common subword strings (especially short suffixes or affixes like “ide,” “ial,” “al/​all,” “no/​on,” “is,” etc.) appear, regardless of the word’s meaning or the surrounding context.

explanations.explanation: This feature lights up on words that single out or rank something as unique or at an extreme (e.g. only, closest/nearest, highest, greater), marking exclusivity or superlative/comparative assertions.

This feature fires on the “head” pieces of content‐bearing tokens—i.e. the morphemic roots of words (rotary ← rotate, car- in carving, cit- in citable, slipp- in slippage, ad in “ad litem,” digit- in digital, etc.) and on stand-alone alphanumeric identifiers (figure/section/case numbers, file‐format codes like gff, area codes like 303, instruction set sizes like 512, acronyms like NPS, Data, camwest, etc.). It thus marks the subword that carries the core semantic load of domain‐specific terms and labels.

This feature is a focus/exclusivity marker detector – it lights up on words like “only,” “just,” and their negated forms (“not only,” “not just,” etc.), signaling a restriction or contrastive narrowing of scope.
